title: Xerophthalmia: The Clinical Spectrum of Vitamin A Deficiency
summary: Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) remains a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide. This guide covers the pathophysiology, staged ocular manifestations, and the WHO-mandated treatment protocols for managing this systemic nutritional crisis.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Vitamin A (Retinol) is critical for the synthesis of rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors and the maintenance of corneal and conjunctival epithelial integrity. Deficiency results in squamous metaplasia and keratinization of ocular surface epithelia, eventually leading to stromal necrosis (keratomalacia).

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Presence of Keratomalacia (Corneal liquefactive necrosis) - Ocular Emergency!
Measles infection (often precipitates rapid corneal decompensation in VAD).

sections.title: WHO Treatment Protocol
content: Day 1: 200,000 IU Vitamin A orally (100,000 IU for 6-12 mo infants, 50,000 IU for <6 mo).
Day 14: Repeat the same dose (if active eye disease or severe malnutrition present).
For vomiting or malabsorption: Inject 100,000 IU IM Vitamin A.

content.explanation: Bitot's spots, Conjunctival xerosis, Keratomalacia, Keratinization.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Bitot's spots are triangular, foamy deposits of keratinized epithelium, typically temporal to the limbus.
Night blindness (Nyctalopia) is usually the earliest functional symptom.
Impression cytology is the gold standard diagnostic for subclinical disease.
Always screen for systemic Vitamin A deficiency in children with chronic diarrhea or measles.
